Good Strategy Bad Strategy - A Five-Minute Masterclass

This book is not a pep talk about vision and ambition, it is a hard look at why most so-called strategies are not strategies at all. Rumelt's promise is simple, diagnose your real problem clearly and you can design a strategy that actually solves it, instead of a document full of nice words that solves nothing.

1. The kernel. Every good strategy has 3 parts, a diagnosis of the challenge, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and a set of coherent actions that carry it out. Before you write a single goal, force yourself through all 3 in order. Skip the diagnosis and everything after it collapses.

2. Diagnosis comes first. You cannot design a strategy for a problem you have not named. Write, in plain language, what is actually happening and why, stripped of hope and spin. A sharp diagnosis simplifies a messy situation into the 1 or 2 things that matter most, and that simplification is most of the work.

3. Bad strategy is fluff. Watch for documents dressed up in restated obvious facts and high-sounding jargon that sound smart but commit to nothing. If you cannot translate a sentence into a plain, testable claim, cut it. Fluff exists to make weak thinking look strong, so treat every buzzword as a red flag.

4. Face the challenge honestly. Bad strategy often comes from leaders who refuse to identify the obstacle because naming it means admitting a hard tradeoff. Say out loud what is actually standing in your way, even if it implicates your own past decisions. You cannot out-plan a problem you will not name.

5. Goals are not strategy. Setting a target, like doubling revenue or becoming number 1, feels like strategy but is not, it is just a wish with a number attached. A real strategy explains the specific actions that will close the gap between where you are and that goal. Next time someone hands you a goal, ask for the plan underneath it.

6. The guiding policy. This is your overall approach for dealing with the diagnosed challenge, it channels action in a chosen direction without dictating every detail. A good guiding policy rules out a vast number of options so your team can move fast on the ones that remain. Write yours as a stance, not a slogan, something like we win on service in the 3 accounts we can dominate, not we will be the best.

7. Coherent action. Strategy fails when different parts of the organization pull in different directions, each optimizing its own piece. Your policies, resources, and actions have to reinforce each other like a chain, not sit side by side as an unrelated list. Check every initiative against the guiding policy, if it does not support the same push, drop it.

8. Find your leverage. Leverage is the place where a focused, well-timed push produces an outsized result, usually at a pivot point or a moment of change in your market. Look for where a competitor is overcommitted, where a capability is undervalued, or where a rule is about to change. Put your energy there instead of spreading it evenly across every front.

9. Set proximate objectives. Instead of chasing a distant, fuzzy vision, pick a target close enough that you can see how to reach it with the resources you have now. A proximate objective is specific, achievable, and creates a foothold you build the next move from. Win the close fight first, the distant vision takes care of itself once you are moving.

10. Concentrate through focus. Power comes from concentrating resources and effort on a decisive point rather than covering every base adequately. Ask where a modest advantage, applied with full force, beats an even effort spread thin. Say no to initiatives that dilute your main push, even good ones, because focus is what makes leverage work.

The through-line here is discipline over enthusiasm. Good strategy is not the boldest vision or the biggest goal, it is the product of an honest diagnosis, a clear guiding policy, and actions that actually reinforce each other toward a specific point of leverage.

Bad strategy hides behind fluff, dodges the real obstacle, and mistakes a wish for a plan. Good strategy does the opposite, it names the problem, picks the fight it can win, and throws its full weight behind that 1 move.

So the next time you sit down to plan, skip the mission statement and start with the diagnosis. Name the actual obstacle in 1 sentence, pick the proximate objective that removes it, and commit your resources to that single point instead of a dozen good intentions.
